faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Freehold Borough basement are from rats?

Around Freehold's downtown blocks the basement evidence shows first in the buildings that share a wall with a food business, and the run usually enters at an old shared utility chase. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Freehold Borough.wildlife_intro:
Freehold Borough is Monmouth's county seat, a compact historic town of Victorians and colonials around Main Street, older twins on the side streets, and the courthouse and county offices at its center. The housing is old and the borough is surrounded by township farmland and horse country, which keeps the edges stocked. Raccoons den in the borough chimneys, bats hold the big attics near the center, squirrels work the street trees, rats appear around the downtown food blocks, and groundhogs commute in from the field edges on every side.

Masonry chimneys deserve a slow look. Mortar joints crumble at the crown, flashing lifts where the stack meets the roof, and an uncapped flue reads to a raccoon like a hollow tree. Sealing here is masonry work as much as animal work: a correctly sized cap, repointed joints where they have failed, and flashing reset so water stays out along with the wildlife. Brick and stone stacks on older houses often hide a second, unused flue that nobody remembers — exactly the sort of quiet, warm shaft a denning animal chooses in March. Freehold's chimneys are the borough's front door for wildlife, and a fitted cap, matched to the stack, closes more future jobs here than any other single item.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Middletown Township deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. In the bayshore villages an opossum under the house is practically a utility, and the marsh-side crawl openings are where Middletown's screening work concentrates. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Middletown Township garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. Inland in Lincroft the gardens sit against wood lines and old field edges, and the groundhog den is reliably in that edge, a short commute from the beds it raids. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

Middletown Township.wildlife_intro:
Middletown is one of New Jersey's biggest townships, and it contains multitudes: bayshore villages like Belford, Port Monmouth, and Leonardo along Sandy Hook Bay, and big inland subdivisions in Lincroft and River Plaza. The bayshore homes sit a street or two from marsh, and raccoons, opossums, and skunks commute out of the wetlands into their crawlspaces and chimneys. Inland, the wooded Lincroft lots give squirrels, raccoons, and groundhogs the standard suburban rotation, with bats in the older homes throughout. One township, two wildlife economies.

Waterfront houses fight moisture on every front. Crawlspaces on pilings, bulkhead walls, and dock structures give raccoons and opossums dry travel lanes straight to the floor system, and salt air eats vent screens and fasteners years faster than it does inland. Materials matter here: stainless and heavy-gauge mesh, sealed penetrations where pipes pass through the foundation, and caps that survive storm wind. Bats favor the warm, still air under raised houses and inside their roof voids. A shore house proofed with inland materials is a shore house scheduled for a second visit. Middletown's bayshore work is specified for salt air and marsh water, while the inland work is specified for canopy and acreage, and the quote names which standard a house is getting.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Howell Township foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. Howell's light soil lets a groundhog move serious earth, and the fans of fresh digging at a shed's back corner in April mean the system is already under the floor. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

Howell's range is set by lot size as much as by animals: a subdivision squirrel job and a five-acre farmstead with groundhogs, skunks, and a barn loft of raccoons are both Howell quotes, of very different shapes. Howell Township.wildlife_intro:
Howell is a big, spreading township along Route 9: postwar neighborhoods, newer subdivisions, working farms, and the Manasquan Reservoir's woods and water at its heart. The northern edge is suburban Monmouth; the southern lots shade into Pine Barrens sand and pitch pine. Groundhogs are Howell's signature call, digging under sheds and foundations in the light soil everywhere. Raccoons and squirrels fill the subdivisions, skunks work the lawns, bats take the farmhouse attics, and the reservoir woods keep a deep bench of animals in circulation.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. Howell yards are big enough to hold a whole burrow system out of sight, so the ground survey here covers the full lot, fence lines and wood lines included.

faqs.q: I found bat droppings in my Neptune Township attic — what happens next?
faqs.a: First we confirm the colony's size and find every entry, which is usually a cluster of small gaps at the ridge, a gable vent, or lifted flashing rather than one obvious hole. Ocean Grove's little attics run hot and still in July, and a colony can occupy one for seasons before the cottage's owners, who may visit monthly, ever smell it. Exclusion happens inside the NJ Fish & Wildlife guideline windows — April 1 to May 14 or August 1 to October 15 — using one-way exits, and the guano cleanup afterward is handled as a health material, bagged out rather than swept into the air.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Neptune Township chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. The Grove's chimneys are as decorative as its porches, and spring raccoon mothers pick the widest, quietest flues on the street; the caps fitted here are sized to vanish into the detail. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

Neptune Township.wildlife_intro:
Neptune Township pairs two famous neighbors: Ocean Grove, the Victorian camp-meeting community of tiny cottages and gingerbread homes inside Neptune's borders, and the older residential streets around the Shark River and the Asbury Park line. Ocean Grove's housing is a wildlife puzzle of its own, small, old, tightly packed houses with complex little rooflines where raccoons and bats find endless entries. The Shark River side adds marsh-edge opossums and raccoons, and the township's older singles and twins give squirrels and skunks steady work all year.

The attic is where most of the damage hides. Droppings foul insulation until it stops insulating, urine soaks ceiling drywall, and nesting shreds stored boxes and wiring jackets. A proper attic job pairs the removal itself with a cleanup decision — spot-cleaning a light mess, or pulling and replacing badly fouled insulation once the animals are out and the entries are sealed. Bat guano gets handled as a health material, bagged and carried out rather than swept dry. Homeowners see photographs of what we found, so the cleanup scope is a choice, not a surprise. Ocean Grove attics are small, layered, and hard to reach, so the inspection here is methodical and photographed, because a missed corner in a cottage roof is next spring's colony.
